title: Balak: dwelling alone (Numbers 23:9)
hookLine: Balaam sees "a people that shall dwell alone"

lines: THE ONLY ONE AT THE TABLE.
FROM THE TOP OF THE ROCKS.
cards: Remember being the only one at the table who didn't eat something, or the only kid who left early on Friday, or the one whose holidays fell on different days from everyone else's?
Being different can feel like standing in a doorway while everyone else is already inside. Balaam's very first blessing has a line about that.
From the top of the rocks he looks down at Israel's camp, and he sees a people that doesn't blend in. He means it as a blessing.

teach.b: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Balaam says: "it is a people that shall dwell alone, And shall not be reckoned among the nations." In Hebrew, am levadad yishkon. A people that dwells by itself.
Readers have heard this line in very different keys.

Some hear a promise: a small people will keep its own shape through history, its own Sabbath, its own calendar, its own language of prayer, and won't simply dissolve into whatever empire is passing through.

Others hear something heavier, an ache that runs through Jewish history, of being set apart whether you chose it or not. Serious people have held both, and the verse doesn't settle it. But here's a detail worth knowing.
The same Hebrew root, badad, alone, shows up at the very end of the Torah, in Moses' last blessing.
There it sits beside the word for safety: Israel dwells in safety, alone. In that verse, being alone isn't exile. It's security, like a house with its own walls.
Some readers draw a difference from that pairing. Lonely means cut off.

teach.h: ALONE MEANS WHOLE, NOT CUT OFF.
teach.b: Alone, in this sense, means whole: having a center of your own, so you can sit at anyone's table without losing yourself. Balaam was hired to curse.
Looking down from the rocks, he saw a people who didn't need to be like everyone else to be all right. Gift or burden, the tradition kept the line, and still reads it aloud every summer.

how: Balaam's first oracle is read in the portion of Balak in summer, and the phrase 'a people that dwells alone' is often quoted in Jewish discussions of identity and history.

games.q: you're Balaam on the first hilltop, paid to curse. you see a people that doesn't blend in. what do you call it?
o: their weakness: they have no allies.
a blessing: a people that dwells alone.
a danger to everyone around them.
games.why: he calls it a blessing: a people that shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations.

practice: Think of something about you that doesn't match the people around you: a practice you keep, a food you skip, a belief, an accent, the way you spend your weekends.
If it usually feels like something to explain, try holding it for a moment as a blessing instead, a center of your own. You don't have to love it; just let it be part of you.
